new_statements.rule_in_words: A single blanket remark in the handbook's pronunciation guide, covering 'most Western Australian Aboriginal languages' collectively: word stress is usually on the first syllable. Nothing is said about Wajarri stress specifically; the Wajarri entry (4.3.11) is a bibliographic/sociolinguistic profile (names, classification, dialects, speaker numbers, researchers, spelling system, materials) with no phonology. It points to Douglas (1981) 'Watjarri', pp. 197-272 in Dixon & Blake (eds) Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 2, as the grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the generic statement is hedged with 'usually' and is not language-specific
new_statements.identity_note: Thieberger 4.3.11 (pp. 92-94) treats Wajarri (Douglas's spelling 'Watjarri'/'Witjari'; also Wadjari, Yamaji, Batiga, Cheangwa, Waiawonga, Wajeri, etc.) as one language located from the head of the Lyons River / Upper Gascoyne through the Murchison, with local groups Yapurtu (northern dialect), Wanmala, Mulyara, Bidungu (Morphy 1985) and Douglas's two dialects 'light Wajarri' (Byro side) vs 'heavy' or katja; Nanu to the north shares 70% vocabulary. No stress information is given for any dialect. The catalog's placement presumably rests on Douglas (1981), which this handbook cites as the only full description.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Douglas 1981:206-207, sec. 2.1.4) is present verbatim in the full-text file we hold, including the sentence truncated in the record ('In words of more than four syllables, secondary stress falls on the penultimate'); the record's evidence note ('search snippets only', 'not re-opened') can be upgraded to full-text-confirmed against the open-access ANU PDF. (2) The stress placement coded per word length as 10 110 1010 10010 100010 (1 = a stressed syllable) is a faithful literal rendering of Douglas: initial primary; secondary on syllable 2 in trisyllables, syllable 3 in quadrisyllables, penult in longer words. The contra note against StressTyp2 (which has 100 for trisyllables) is correctly stated. sources.note: Only modern first-hand description (Marmion has worked on Wajarri since the 1990s); our classification rests on Douglas 1981's four-sentence impressionistic statement, whose trisyllable claim (secondary stress on syllable 2, i.e. a 1-2 clash, coded 110) is typologically odd and is exactly where StressTyp2 departed from the source (100). A 2023 phonology paragraph would settle 110 vs 100 vs alternating 101.
